title: Parent guide to supporting digital SAT and ACT prep
summary: Learn how parents can support students preparing for the digital SAT and ACT with practical routines, realistic expectations, and effective study habits.
body_markdown:
With Acely's Parent Portal, you can manage your family's account directly, including your billing and subscription. You can also check in on your student's progress with our activity feed that shows what they've been working on.


Our Parent Portal makes it easier for you to support your student as they're studying and to celebrate the wins along the way.


If your teen has a documented anxiety disorder or learning difference, absolutely. Extended time is the most common accommodation and can make a meaningful difference. The application process through College Board (SAT) and ACT takes several weeks, so start early, ideally at least 3 months before the test date. Both[SAT accommodations](https://acely.com/sat-prep/sat-accomodations) and[ACT accommodations](https://acely.com/act-prep/act-accommodations) have dedicated guides on Acely walking through the process step by step.


Yes, and at the most selective schools they matter more than they did a few years ago. A growing number of top universities have reinstated testing requirements for the 2026-2027 cycle after several pandemic-era years of test-optional policy, and even at schools that remain test-optional, submitting a strong score tends to help an application rather than hurt it. Scores also frequently gate merit scholarships at the state and institutional level, regardless of whether a school's general admissions policy is test-optional.


Acely's[college admissions hub](https://acely.com/college-admissions) breaks down how scores factor into the process at different types of schools, and the[SAT score guide](https://acely.com/sat-prep/sat-score-guide) and[ACT score guide](https://acely.com/act-prep/act-score-guide) cover what counts as a competitive score for specific target schools.


Earlier is almost always better, but the sweet spot for most students is 3 to 6 months before their target test date. Starting early means your teen can study at a sustainable pace, one practice test per week with consistent daily sessions, rather than cramming everything into the final few weeks. If your teen is a sophomore, now is a great time to start building the habit even before committing to a specific test date.


Most guidance caps it at two to three sittings. Repeated sittings without a change in preparation between them tend to produce diminishing, not compounding, returns, and colleges that superscore reward a different, more targeted approach on each attempt over simply testing more often.


Acely's[SAT retake guide](https://acely.com/sat-prep/sat-retakes-superscores) and[ACT retake guide](https://acely.com/act-prep/act-retake-guide) cover how to decide if and when a retake is worth it, and how to prep differently the second or third time around so each attempt actually moves the score.


Score fluctuation between practice tests is normal and expected, not a sign that prep isn't working. Section-by-section variance, fatigue, unfamiliar question types, and the way the digital SAT and Enhanced ACT scale raw answers into section scores can all cause swings of 20 to 60 points between sittings even when underlying skill is trending up.


Acely's[score fluctuation guide](https://acely.com/parent-resources/sat-act-score-fluctuation) walks through why this happens and how to read a trend instead of a single score; the practical takeaway is to track a rolling average across 3 to 4 practice tests rather than reacting to any one result.
